source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's DFW1 campus in Carrollton, Texas publishes 45 MW of IT capacity across 600,000 square feet of technical space, and that figure is the operator's own.

The number matters because it is one of the few in Texas that can be counted at all. Texas holds 137 mapped facilities, but only 19 publish a megawatt figure, and those 19 total 475.41 MW. DFW1's 45 MW ranks third among them. The gap between 137 mapped and 19 publishing is the pattern: most of the state's data center capacity is invisible to any count that can be made from published specs, and this campus is an exception.

For AI specifically, published IT capacity is the input that converts a building into a ceiling on compute. A 45 MW facility sets an upper bound on how many accelerators can run inside it, though the bound depends entirely on rack density. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 45 MW is roughly 1,125 racks. At 130 kW per rack, plausible for dense liquid-cooled deployment, it is about 346. Neither figure is stated by CyrusOne, and the spec page publishes no rack count, no rack density, and no cooling method, so accelerator count cannot be derived from this data.

The certifications, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, SSAE 16 Type II, and TIA-942, qualify the campus to host payment card data, protected health data, federal information systems, and audited financial controls. TIA-942 speaks to the physical topology of the facility. None of them name a customer, and the page publishes no address, no postal code, and no tenant list, so nothing here says who runs inside it. What the data does not cover is equally clear: no power source, no utility, no interconnection queue position, and no expansion plan. The 45 MW is a capacity figure, not a statement about how much of it is energized or contracted.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
